newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lebed briefs PM but hints at lack of support.
newsitem.headline: Lebed briefs PM but hints at lack of support.

text.p: Kremlin security chief Alexander Lebed met Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Wednesday to brief him on talks with Chechen separatists, which Lebed said had succeeded in smoothing over a number of disputes.

But he admitted it was hard to shake off the impression he was not getting much support in Moscow, where top officials, including Lebed and Chernomyrdin, appear to be jostling for influence as President Boris Yeltsin prepares for heart surgery.
Asked by Interfax news agency who in Moscow was slowing the peace process, Lebed replied: "Who's backing me these days?"

"Unfortunately, representatives of the organs of the state have taken up a strange position," the straight-talking former paratroop general said. "They do nothing constructive and are trying to occupy themselves with criticism."

Aides to Chernomyrdin, to whom Yeltsin has handed some security responsibilities, said he met Lebed for 40 minutes but would say only that they discussed Tuesday's meeting in Chechnya between Lebed and separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev.

Lebed had been quoted earlier as saying Chernomyrdin should give a helping hand to attempts to get feuding pro- and anti-Moscow Chechen factions to form a coalition government and to start releasing federal funds for postwar reconstruction.
"By the end of the week, Viktor Chernomyrdin will get personally involved in the negotiating process," he was quoted as saying before meeting the prime minister.

Yeltsin, in a Moscow clinic for tests ahead of his bypass operation, discussed Chechnya with his influential chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais. The president has not met Lebed, who says his peace deal on August 31 ended the war, since he named him his personal envoy to Chechnya more than a month ago.

Lebed, a 46-year-old political newcomer with overt presidential ambitions, has agreed with the separatists to defer debate on their demands for secession for five years in return for a Russian troop withdrawal and a ceasefire.

Yeltsin publicly backed him but questioned the need to pull out troops immediately. Chernomyrdin congratulated the president's envoy but undercut him by insisting the deal was not binding and ruling out any question of Chechen independence.
The communist opposition also hit out at Lebed for failing to spell out that Russia would never give Chechnya up.

Even Russian army commanders in the region seem to have felt free to ignore the peace deal. General Vyacheslav Tikhomirov halted the troop withdrawal almost as soon as it began last week over disputes with the rebels about the exchange of prisoners.
Lebed was quoted as saying on Wednesday he was "fed up" with such attitutes but said Tikhomirov would restart the pull-out.
Lebed's next move is unclear. Some commentators say Yeltsin may be virtually ignoring him now his original function -- helping the president win reelection -- has been fulfilled.
Chubais told Izvestia newspaper on Wednesday that Lebed had not been "shoved into a corner" and insisted he, Lebed and Chernomyrdin were working together to end the Chechen crisis.
But the Security Council, of which Lebed is secretary, issued a statement on Tuesday hitting back at critics of Lebed's Chechen policy and work on other, unrelated, security matters.

Some analysts see Lebed's public attack last week on the government's budget and his first foreign assignment, to Belarus, as evidence he wants to broaden his brief and avoid his career being solely dependent on fragile gains in Chechnya.
